cases.title: Intake and Handoffs, Automated
cases.p1_html: Problem. Creative requests arrived by too many routes, and final assets (design links, copy docs, images) got lost as work moved between related tasks. Native syncing across task levels wasn't available in our setup.
cases.p2_html: What I did. I co-designed and co-built our Asana implementation for marketing requests from scratch, with the team that runs intake, and I handled the technical build. Before writing any automation code, I had Claude Code interview me and test whether the platform could support the idea. Then I built Asana Tasks Family Sync: a rule that carries final assets between related tasks, is safe to re-run, copies cleanly to other projects, and is documented. I paired it with team training so it stuck. Result. Final assets, including design links, copy docs, and video, now follow the work automatically, so nobody has to hunt for the latest file.

about_page.lead: I've always lived in two worlds at once. I'm the nerd who ran IT for a retreat center in Vermont, tested software, and answered support tickets, and I still can't leave a repetitive task alone. I'm also a maker: I write and play music, I've produced video for years, and I love a good pipeline. The two have run side by side the whole way. When they line up, I build things like an Asana setup that keeps creative work from getting lost, or a pipeline that cuts footage while I'm at the park with my family. When they don't, I'm the one in the room who speaks both languages.

about.text: Where I Live
When I was a kid, I heard Steve Jobs describe Apple as sitting at the intersection of arts and technology, and I've tried to live there ever since.

I can't just write music. I need to develop concepts, produce them, and collect the gear that records it. I can't just edit video. I need to pitch ideas and build the pipeline that saves hours of my time, so I can play with my family at the park, and still publish on a steady cadence!
I've onboarded, trained, and mentored new team members. I lead with care, kindness, and a sense of humor, because people do their best work when they feel looked after.

experiments.text: In plain English: Waves is a local LLM inference stack I designed and built with AI-assisted development (vibe coding). Three machines, four lanes, specialized models, and no cloud dependency, with a searchable index over my own notes and files.
Why the name: Sound waves, brain waves, energy, motion, and carrying the whole team. When the models focus together, that's clarity.

How it fits: small collectors watch for changes, rules react instantly, a filter drops anything unchanged, and then the models focus together as Waves: they cross-check each other and one writes the summary.
What it taught me: treat AI like infrastructure, with owners, fallbacks, and cost limits.
Built with: a 27B reasoning model, a 9B vision model, MCP servers, and Meilisearch.

A 27B reasoning model on a 24 GB GPU, a 9B vision model on a 12 GB GPU, prefix KV-cache pinning for fast first responses, custom MCP servers, and Meilisearch for search, and nomic embed on the Dell OptiPlex for embeddings. Three machines, four lanes.
Small collectors that watch for changes. No model needed.
Instant rules, like stepping aside when I open my video editor.
Filters out anything that hasn't changed.
Turns what changed into a short brief.
All the models, focusing together. That's clarity.
Waves, layer by layer, on three machines and four lanes.

In plain English: Clarity is the friendly, curious agent on top of Waves. She asks good questions before she gives answers, and she runs on whichever local model I've swapped in. Her shape is a small cousin of the studio mark: a little web that turns to look at whoever is talking. Move your cursor, or tap, and she'll find you.
Talk to her: I can talk to Clarity from my phone through Siri, and she can kick off automations, including Home Assistant ones. A voice front door on top of Waves.
What it taught me: good questions beat fast answers, in AI and in intake.
Reasoning on a 27B local model, speech with Kokoro, search with Meilisearch, served with FastAPI. First words arrive in about 180 ms on my hardware with a warm cache.
A condensed example of how I work with Clarity. Details are simplified for the page.

In plain English: APPA is software that turns raw multi-camera footage into editable timelines for Premiere Pro and DaVinci Resolve. I built it as producer of Ben Windle Shoots His Shot to replace roughly 15 to 20 hours a week of manual logging and rough cutting. Time saved now: measuring.

The Showrunner: before APPA assembles a rough cut, a Showrunner pass compares a new shoot with the pacing of my best-performing shorts: how fast the cuts come, how soon the hook lands, and which story beats carry the joke. It acts as a developmental editor before I open Premiere or Resolve.
What it taught me: the hours leak in logging and rough cuts, not in creativity.
Built with: WhisperX, PySceneDetect, OpenTimelineIO, and FCPXML.
Seeing lane picks the best candidates
Showrunner compares with my best shorts
24fps .fcpxml and .otio timelines, plus a review proxy
APPA runs across all four Waves lanes.
I break things on my own time so I can be careful on yours.
What it taught me: scope AI work like any project, with small steps and a stop rule.
The Agents That Flooded My To-Do List
I wired automation and overnight scripts straight into my personal task board.
They created well over a hundred tickets, most of everything on the board, and a reminder loop nagged me for hours.
Agents get their own queue. Humans own the board.
I added scroll effects on top of one giant navigation script instead of refactoring it.
Several effects fought each other, the browser froze, headers duplicated inside frames, and I broke my own live layouts.
Refactor first, run one engine, and set a performance budget before adding motion.
I edited my site's HTML with blind find-and-replace scripts.
Tags broke, text doubled, and CSS vanished.
Content lives in a CMS, and a scrub check runs before every commit.
I let an image model and unranked photo queries pick the hero art for a daily digest.
I got generic AI slop, screenshots, and photos of doorframes.
A four-step editorial hierarchy, a vision model that grades candidates, and a human veto.
